title: Some flames burn at only about 400 °C and are almost too faint to see

cover.alt: A glowing white ball of flame burning in the dark inside an experiment chamber on the International Space Station.

body: In an ordinary flame, fuel molecules are smashed into small fragments that burn all the way to carbon dioxide, and the temperature climbs by around **1,000 °C**. In a **cool flame** the fuel only partly reacts: the fragments stay large and recombine, so little heat, light or CO₂ comes out and the temperature rises by just a few tens of degrees. Their faint pale-blue glow comes from excited formaldehyde molecules. Humphry Davy stumbled on them in the 1810s, and they can help set off knocking in car engines.

slides.alt: Inside a dark experiment chamber on the International Space Station, a gas flame lights with a bright flash, settles into a glowing white ball and slowly dims.
slides.caption: A test flame on the space station lights, glows as a ball and dims. The cool flame that followed, once it seemed to go out, was too faint to see as it happened.
slides.music: “Stay the Course” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

left.label: Hot flame
left.text: Fuel breaks into small pieces that burn fully to CO₂. The temperature rises by around 1,000 °C, with plenty of light.

right.label: Cool flame
right.text: Fuel breaks into large pieces that recombine. The temperature rises by a few tens of degrees, with a faint blue glow.

slides.prompt: Cool flames are rare in daily life, but they cause trouble in one everyday machine. Which one?
slides.detail: Cool flames can help start engine knock, when the last pocket of fuel and air ignites on its own. Antiknock additives work mainly by removing the radicals involved.

events.text: Humphry Davy discovers cool flames by accident
Harry Emeléus, who first recorded their light, coins the name “cold flame”
A new kind, the cool diffusion flame, is first seen around fuel droplets on the space station

slides.question: What gives a cool flame its faint pale-blue glow?
slides.explanation: The blue light comes from formaldehyde molecules made in an excited state as the fuel partly reacts. Soot is what makes an ordinary candle flame yellow.
